matching.reasoningTemplate: Refractory hypotension in a steroid-dependent patient suggests adrenal crisis.

clinicalPearls: Adrenal crisis typically emerges after a prolonged prodrome of nonspecific complaints rather than appearing out of the blue (p.3111).
Crisis is more frequent in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency because both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion are lost (p.3111).
Postural hypotension can progress to frank hypovolaemic shock (p.3111).
Prospective data: about 8.3 adrenal crises per 100 patient-years and roughly 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis is classified as a form of endocrine/distributive shock (p.2353).
In suspected crisis, it is reasonable to draw a baseline cortisol (and ACTH), start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing — diagnostic testing must never delay treatment (p.3111).

Starting thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient can precipitate adrenal crisis, because thyroid hormone shortens cortisol half-life; screen for adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism in possible polyendocrine syndrome (p.3133).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute adrenal insufficiency reflects an absolute or relative deficiency of cortisol, in primary disease compounded by loss of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decompensate into hypovolaemic shock. Crisis is usually unmasked by a stressor that exceeds the inadequate cortisol reserve — intercurrent illness, surgery or other stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation as in hyperthyroidism (p.3111).
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of distributive/endocrine shock (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) (p.2353)
infectionMimics: Acute abdomen-like presentation with abdominal tenderness, nausea, vomiting and fever can mimic an intra-abdominal infection (p.3111)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute abdomen / surgical abdomen (abdominal pain, tenderness, nausea, vomiting) (p.3111)
Primary neurologic disease — decreased responsiveness progressing to stupor and coma (p.3111)
additionalInvestigations: Baseline serum cortisol AND plasma ACTH drawn before starting steroids, with formal testing deferred (p.3111)
Short cosyntropin (ACTH stimulation) test once stabilised — failure cutoff roughly cortisol <450-500 nmol/L (16-18 ug/dL) at 30-60 min (p.3111)
Plasma renin to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary disease (p.3111)
Adrenal steroid autoantibodies to assess for autoimmune adrenalitis (p.3111)
Adrenal CT for hemorrhage, infiltration or masses if autoantibodies negative (p.3111)
Very-long-chain fatty acids in autoantibody-negative males to exclude X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (p.3111)
Hypothalamic-pituitary MRI when ACTH is inappropriately low (secondary cause) (p.3111)
Associated labs: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, raised creatinine, normochromic anaemia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia (p.3110)
redFlags: Refractory or postural hypotension progressing to hypovolaemic shock (p.3111)
Hyperpigmentation suggesting underlying primary adrenal insufficiency (p.3110)
harrison.prognosis: Acute adrenal insufficiency is potentially lethal (p.636). Even with established care, crises and crisis-related deaths continue to occur (~8.3 crises and ~0.5 deaths per 100 patient-years) (p.3111).
pitfalls: Do NOT let diagnostic testing delay treatment in suspected crisis (p.3111).

Random/baseline serum cortisol has limited diagnostic value because levels may be coincidentally low from normal diurnal rhythm, and many secondary cases have near-normal baseline cortisol that only fails on stimulation testing (p.3111).
Do NOT start thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency — it can precipitate crisis (p.3133).
Hyperthyroidism increases glucocorticoid inactivation and can trigger crisis (p.3111).
Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by concurrent primary hypothyroidism, which prolongs cortisol half-life (p.3133).
